data.title: Tractor Supply joins Uber Marketplace, adding delivery options for rural customers
data.description:
Tractor Supply Co. is adding Uber as a delivery partner, making its products available through the Uber, Uber Eats and Postmates apps. The companies announced the nationwide partnership Nov. 12.

Customers can order pet food, animal care products, lawn and garden supplies, tools and outdoor gear for on-demand delivery. Tractor Supply operated 2,486 stores in 49 states as of Sept. 26, along with 135 Petsense by Tractor Supply stores. The announcement refers to Tractor Supply’s stores, not Petsense locations.

Tractor Supply is No. 83 in the Top 1000 Database. The database tracks North America’s largest online retailers, ranking them by annual ecommerce sales and more.

Tractor Supply expands delivery beyond metro areas

Uber’s pitch centers on geography. Tractor Supply stores are concentrated in rural, exurban and suburban communities, which Uber sees as an opportunity to extend on-demand delivery beyond major cities.

“The need for convenience doesn’t stop at the city limits,” said Nathan Bernheim, Uber’s head of retail partnerships, in the announcement.

Matthew Rubin, Tractor Supply’s senior vice president and president of digital and ecommerce, said the deal gives customers more ways to shop. It also introduces the retailer to “millions of Uber users” who may not have shopped there before, he said. “Tractor Supply is continually finding new ways to serve customers and make Life Out Here more convenient,” Rubin added.

Customers can search for Tractor Supply in the Uber, Uber Eats or Postmates app, or browse the Retail section. They then pick a store, build a cart, choose a delivery option and track the order in the app. 

To mark the launch, Uber is offering $20 off Tractor Supply orders of $60 or more. Fees and terms apply.

The announcement did not specify delivery speeds or fees.

Tractor Supply’s relationship with Instacart and DoorDash

Uber is the second delivery platform Tractor Supply added this year. In July, the retailer announced it had joined Instacart Marketplace, a competitor to Uber. 

At the time of the announcement, Tractor Supply and Instacart representatives shared similar sentiments about expanding same-day delivery to rural customers and introducing Tractor Supply to new shoppers.

Tractor Supply has also had a delivery partnership with DoorDash since 2022. Now the delivery market is consolidating. 

On Oct. 29, DoorDash announced that it would acquire Instacart in a deal valued at $17 billion. The deal needs regulatory and Instacart shareholder approval. The companies expect it to close near the end of 2027 or in the first half of 2028.

Until then, Instacart will operate independently. DoorDash expects to keep the Instacart brand, app and enterprise technology products afterward.

Tractor Supply’s own delivery network

The Uber deal builds on a store-based delivery network Tractor Supply has spent the past year and a half expanding. CEO Hal Lawton said in September that the retailer has offered delivery from stores for five or six years, including same-day and two- to three-day options. Its newer “Final Mile” system links every three to four stores in a hub-and-spoke arrangement, with one store serving four.

Tractor Supply completed as many last-mile deliveries in the first half of 2026 as it did in all of 2025, Lawton said. Delivery from stores led double-digit digital sales growth in fiscal Q2, even as comparable store sales fell 1.5% in a difficult quarter.

The retailer is also building out its supply chain. In September, Tractor Supply opened its 11th distribution center in Nampa, Idaho, an 865,000-square-foot facility that will support 123 stores across nine states in its first year. The center was designed to serve more than 200 stores at full capacity.

data.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet for AI purchases through retailer checkouts
data.description:
OpenAI is giving its artificial intelligence (AI) shopping agents a way to pay through retailers’ checkout systems, marking another shift in the ChatGPT maker’s evolving agentic commerce strategy.

Launched Nov. 13 in partnership with American Express, Chase, Mastercard and Visa, ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s “always-on” personal agents, known as dots, complete purchases on shoppers’ behalf.

Rather than keeping transactions inside ChatGPT, the virtual wallet works through merchants’ existing checkouts. Businesses retain their customer relationships, along with “control over pricing, fulfillment, returns, and customer service,” OpenAI said in its announcement.

For now, Wallet is rolling out to a limited number of U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers. While shoppers can add a payment card for agents to use, they must still approve each purchase before a transaction can be completed. The company has yet to identify any specific retailers accepting ChatGPT Wallet transactions.

Alongside the launch, OpenAI also released a Commerce Partner Playbook aimed at helping businesses prepare for a future of more agent-led purchases.

How ChatGPT Wallet works

The launch follows a change in OpenAI’s checkout plans earlier this year. After introducing Instant Checkout in September 2025, the company shifted toward transactions through merchant apps in March.

ChatGPT Wallet builds on that approach. “We’re building agent-led commerce to fit reliably into existing systems,” OpenAI said in its announcement.

According to the company, roughly 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT each week, including consumers researching and comparing products. Wallet aims to take that shopping activity a step further, allowing agents to complete purchases, it said.

Before checkout, shoppers review the items, total and payment card. They then authorize the purchase through a security check, such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan.

Once approved, the payment network generates a tokenized credential in place of the customer’s actual card details. Neither the merchant nor the AI agent receives those credentials, OpenAI said.

“Users keep their card’s existing rewards and protections for eligible disputes with businesses, for example when an item is defective,” the company added. Banks and payment networks, meanwhile, continue evaluating transactions.

By starting with a limited rollout, OpenAI said it hopes to “learn from real-world use” and improve compatibility with businesses and payment providers.

Eventually, the company expects users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agents, with limits on spending, product categories or time periods. OpenAI said those transactions would still require “enhanced safeguards,” including biometric checks and records of authorization.

What ChatGPT Wallet means for online retailers

Keeping checkout in retailers’ hands may address one concern about agentic commerce. But that doesn’t mean every business is ready — or willing — to accept purchases made by AI agents.

Amazon, for example, blocked Meta’s Muse AI agent from shopping on its website in September, citing unauthorized activity and privacy and security concerns.

Other retailers may block legitimate transactions unintentionally. OpenAI acknowledged that existing security and fraud prevention systems can interfere with agent-led purchases.

Its new Commerce Partner Playbook offers guidance on making products accessible to agents and supporting payments through existing systems.

For starters, retailers can claim and verify their businesses in ChatGPT, then provide current product information, including pricing and availability.

But making products discoverable doesn’t guarantee agents can access a website. Retailers may need to configure their content delivery networks (CDNs) or firewalls to recognize signed requests through Web Bot Auth, a method for verifying AI agent identities. According to OpenAI, browser access doesn’t require a plugin or product feed.

Payment acceptance presents another hurdle. Fraud detection tools may flag legitimate agent purchases, leading to declined or canceled transactions.

To reduce those risks, OpenAI said it is working with payment providers Adyen, Checkout.com and Stripe, along with fraud prevention companies Forter, Riskified, Sardine and Signifyd.

Merchants can also add WebMCP tools or plugins to “let agents check availability, manage carts, or take other actions” through existing systems, the company said.

Payment companies expand their agentic commerce efforts

ChatGPT Wallet arrives as payment networks develop their own tools for AI-initiated transactions.

In April, Visa introduced Intelligent Commerce Connect, offering businesses a single integration for agent-led transactions. It followed in June with a partnership to bring Visa’s payment capabilities into OpenAI experiences.

Mastercard, meanwhile, introduced Agent Connect in September to connect merchants with AI agents, digital platforms and payment providers.

The push extends beyond consumer shopping. In October, Visa, BILL and Billtrust launched a live pilot enabling authorized AI agents to complete approved invoice payments through supplier portals.

data.title: eBay adds visual identification to listing generation options
data.description:
Ebay has been building out features for its seller-focused “magical listing tool” for years, and the latest options to debut include a workflow that takes a user directly from their own photo to an artificial intelligence (AI)-generated listing.

The online marketplace announced the new feature on Nov. 11, sharing that it would be available in Australia, France, Germany, Italy, the U.K., and the U.S.

EBay ranks No. 6 in Digital Commerce 360’s Global Online Marketplaces Database. The market research tool ranks the 100 largest such marketplaces by third-party gross merchandise value (GMV).

How does eBay’s new visual identification feature work?

The process for sellers to take photos of their items with their own cameras and use those photos to begin creating eBay listings consists of three steps, according to details published in a corporate blog post.

First, the seller needs to take a photo of their item and share it with eBay. Then, the magical listing tool uses AI to identify what’s in the photo and fill out the listing fields. According to eBay, at that point, all the seller needs to do is review their draft for corrections and then publish.

EBay noted that the process builds off of a mobile listing creation flow that it debuted in 2025.

What eBay has added to its magical listing tool over time

“Magical listing is streamlining listing creation and bringing more C2C inventory onto eBay, while AI enhancements to search and discovery are helping buyers more easily find the most relevant items across our 2.6 billion listings,” said eBay CEO Jamie Iannone during the company’s Q2 earnings call in August.

EBay noted in its Nov. 11 announcement that 10 million unique sellers have used AI features on eBay, resulting in 800,000 new listings daily.

“In Q2, we began integrating enhanced pricing guidance into magical listing to help sellers balance velocity and price realization, and we improved the accuracy of package size estimates to help manage shipping costs more efficiently,” Iannone stated.

He previously referenced a “new experience leverages AI agents from the start to autonomously build listings from images alone” in March.

The online marketplace shared more features in April, setting the stage for the latest updates, with options to generate listings from photos and titles. At the time, it noted that testing in the U.K. showed that the AI features “led to a 50% reduction in the total steps needed to list and faster listing times.”

data.title: Asics uses AI-powered drones to recover misplaced inventory 60% faster
data.description:
Asics America Corp. is using autonomous drones to find misplaced merchandise at its primary North American distribution center, a move the company says is helping it curb the risk of unfulfilled orders.

The technology, developed by Corvus Robotics, is helping the sportswear brand recover misplaced inventory about 60% faster, according to a Nov. 10 announcement from the warehouse automation provider.

At Asics’ facility in Byhalia, Mississippi, drones now conduct inventory counts in two key storage areas every month, up from twice annually. The higher frequency lets Asics offer merchandise on online marketplaces that were previously withheld due to fulfillment concerns.

Asics America, based in Irvine, California, is the U.S. subsidiary of Japanese sportswear company Asics Corp.

How Asics uses drones to count warehouse inventory

Asics’ 855,000-square-foot distribution center in Byhalia houses nearly 3 million units of footwear, apparel and accessories across roughly 44,000 stock-keeping units.

The facility fulfills ecommerce orders while also supplying Asics stores and wholesale customers. All three channels draw from the same inventory pool, and customer returns are processed there as well.

Asics is using Corvus One drones in two warehouse zones: a singles area that stores returned merchandise and individual pairs of shoes, and a case reserve area that holds full cartons.

The drones perform seven scheduled flights a night, starting at around 7 p.m., Corvus said. Using onboard computer vision and spatial reasoning, they navigate aisles less than 6 feet wide without needing additional warehouse infrastructure, such as markers or beacons.

During each flight, the drones scan universal product codes while also counting boxes stored at each location. Corvus said the system compares those counts with barcode scans, identifying inventory discrepancies. The following morning, a warehouse employee reviews the results using images and video captured during the flights.

“Now we can just look at the footage and we can tell exactly what’s going on with it in the locations before we have to send someone out,” Angela Williford, inventory control operations manager at Asics America, said in a Corvus video case study. “If it’s something that we can correct from the desk, we’ll correct it then.”

More frequent counts help Asics recover merchandise

During one three-month period, drones identified 26 misplaced cases containing more than 200 pairs of shoes. Without the additional counts, those items could have remained unavailable for sale until the next scheduled inventory review, Asics said.

Koestler estimated that Asics is recovering misplaced inventory roughly 60% faster than before the deployment.

“You don’t want to have to count a thousand locations to find the four or five that have problems,” he said in the video case study.

The automation has also shifted how warehouse employees spend their time. Rather than focusing on routine cycle counts, workers can dedicate more effort to inventory reconciliation, discrepancy investigations and wholesale-support projects, according to the companies.

Corvus also said the drones reduce the need for lift equipment during inventory counts, limiting traffic in the facility’s narrow aisles.

Asics makes more inventory available to marketplaces

The inventory gains have also influenced how Asics sells products through online marketplaces.

Before adopting the drone system, Asics withheld between 12 and 15 units out of every 100 from the inventory feeds it provided to marketplace partners, according to Corvus. The company did so because products shown as available might be missing or difficult to locate when orders arrived.

With monthly counts providing greater visibility into stock levels, Asics said it now publishes its full inventory availability feed.

Corvus said the change allows Asics to offer more merchandise at full price rather than potentially liquidating it at a discount. The companies did not disclose how much additional revenue the change has generated.

Other retailers expand warehouse automation

Asics is among a growing number of companies deploying inventory drones to improve warehouse operations.

After deploying Corvus’ technology, health and wellness retailer GNC increased inventory counts at its distribution centers in Indianapolis and Phoenix, according to a case study. Counts rose to as many as 10 to 12 times per year, up from two to four.

Likewise, Southern Glazer’s Wine & Spirits expanded its drone deployment to nine distribution centers. The beverage distributor reported a 100-basis-point improvement in cases handled per hour, Corvus said.

Other major retailers are investing in different forms of warehouse automation. Walmart Inc. recently announced plans to expand Symbotic automation technology across 25 U.S. regional distribution centers. The retailer said the rollout is designed to support inventory management, increase storage capacity and improve product flow throughout its supply chain.

Walmart ranks No. 2 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 1000 Database. The database tracks North America’s largest online retailers, ranking them by annual ecommerce sales and more.

data.title: GrubMarket launches AI Agent to turn invoices into purchase orders
data.description:
GrubMarket, a South San Francisco, California-based software-as-a-service (SAAS) company working with food producers, wholesalers, distributors and retailers, is expanding its use of artificial intelligence (AI) with a new AI agent. The company designed its new AI agent to turn vendor invoices and receipts into purchase orders for food distributors. The tool, called the “AI Orders – Purchase Order Agent,” was made to reduce the amount of manual data entry required from produce and other fresh food distributors.

“The food supply chain industry is undergoing unprecedented transformation driven by artificial intelligence,” said Mike Xu, CEO of GrubMarket, in a release statement. “With our new AI Orders – Purchase Order Agent, we are bringing powerful AI capabilities to another critical function within food distribution.”

The new agent follows other recent AI rollouts from GrubMarket. In June, the company announced the launch of an AI sales agent. Its other AI deployments have included a reporting AI agent on its GrubAssist AI platform. GrubMarket also created its Monitoring AI Agent that tracks financial and operational data for customers.

Now, the technology provider is turning to purchase orders.

Why GrubMarket launched its new AI agent

Xu said that by automating purchasing workflows, GrubMarket is helping distributors operate more efficiently. In turn, he believes that they can gain better visibility into their businesses, making better-informed decisions and improving profitability.

“This launch represents another important step in our broader vision of building specialized AI agents that automate and optimize every major function across the food supply chain industry,” Xu said, adding that the company remains committed to leveraging artificial intelligence to help businesses modernize their operations and unlock new levels of efficiency and growth.

Industry observers said the real test will be in the details.

Amy Dean, vice president of operations at SC Codeworks, a Columbus, Ohio-based warehouse management software company, said that every company handles purchase order entry differently. However, she sees it is most likely being driven by spreadsheets, ERP systems and planners.

“AI has the potential to reduce repetitive data entry, which would free up employees to handle exceptions, vendor relationships, and more strategic purchasing activities,” Dean said.

She noted AI will need to navigate special challenges that come with the food business.

“Food distribution especially is not always straightforward,” she assessed. “There are many variables that change often, such as recalls, substitutions, and vendor-specific requirements.”

Dean, who is an operations and IT expert with over a decade of experience in logistics, believes that it will be “critical that all of that is accounted for in the logic that is used with an AI agent.”

Moreover, she sees access to accurate data as a vital part of the new agent’s success.

“The ability for an AI agent to read invoices, receipts and photos could be beneficial for organizations that don’t currently utilize integration tools,” Dean stated. “However, that AI agent is only as effective as the data it has access to. This is where inventory accuracy becomes critical and current business processes can make or break the success.”

Larger challenges for the new agent

Dmytro Klymentiev is an AI systems engineer in Chicago who builds AI automation and ERP systems for businesses. He said reading a photo of an invoice and pulling out the line items is no longer the hard part. In his view, that is because most current AI models can do it. What GrubMarket adds, he said, is the connection. The extracted data becomes a structured purchase order inside the distributor’s own system, matched to its catalog.

“That is useful, but I would call it an incremental step rather than a new way of purchasing,” Klymentiev said.

In his view, the time savings are narrower than they look. He pointed out that while nobody needs to type out an order, someone may still need to check each draft to avoid knock-on effects from errors.

“A misread quantity or a wrong product match turns into a wrong order, then a wrong delivery, a failed invoice match and wrong stock levels,” Klymentiev stated. “The work moves from data entry to review, and the review has to be careful.”

Before adopting a tool like this, he recommends that distributors ask whether it flags a line or guesses when it’s unsure, how it matches products to their catalog, what happens with new or renamed items, and whether they can measure its error rate on their own documents before it touches live orders.
